APL synapses project · step-by-step reports · Report 10 · 2026-10-23

Distances along APL between glomeruli

QuestionHow far apart, measured along APL's own arbor, are APL's synapses at the microglomeruli of different glomeruli, and what does that imply for how much a non-spiking APL inhibits a glomerulus's own KCs versus other glomeruli's?
Inputs
  • APL skeletons (SWC): hemibrain v1.2 body 425790257; male CNS v1.0 bodies 10977 (APL_L) and 10540 (APL_R), in data/skeletons/
  • Calyx APL synapse tables with bouton and claw assignments (Reports 01, 02)
  • Derived PN boutons (Report 02)
Outputs
  • apl_geodesic/APL_geodesic_glomerulus_pairs.csv, APL_geodesic_microglomeruli.csv, APL_geodesic_glomerulus_by_subarbor.csv, APL_geodesic_summary.json, figures, and APL_geodesic_notes.md
  • The same under with_outside_ROI_synapses/apl_geodesic/ with synapses outside the official ROIs added
Scripts
  • scripts/apl_geodesic.py
  • scripts/reports/r10_geodesic.py (this report)

APL does not fire action potentials, so a signal entering it at one synapse fades with distance along its neurites. How strongly an input in one place inhibits KCs elsewhere then depends on the path length along APL, not on the straight-line distance. Yang asked (2026-10-23) for this distance between every pair of glomeruli, weighted by synapse counts, for hemibrain and male CNS. This report explains how it is computed and what it shows. Numbers are from the official ROIs; the second version is nearly the same (Section 7).

1Step 1: APL skeletons

A skeleton represents a neuron as a tree of points (nodes) joined by straight segments (edges), each node pointing to a parent. The files are the public FlyEM skeletons. Distances along a tree are unique, because there is exactly one path between two nodes. A few skeletons come in several unconnected pieces. These are joined by the shortest bridges between pieces (a minimum spanning tree over the pieces), and the longest bridge needed is under 3 µm.

2Step 2: which synapses belong to a glomerulus

A microglomerulus is one PN bouton plus the KC claws whose main bouton it is (the bouton that gives the claw most of its PN synapses; Report 02). Its glomerulus is the bouton's PN's glomerulus, uniglomerular PN types only. The APL synapses on it are:

  • APL↔PN synapses on the bouton (partner-side site within 2 µm of the bouton's T-bar cluster), both directions;
  • APL↔KC synapses on those claws (KC-side site within 2 µm of the claw), both directions.
Table 3. Synapses used. Only about a third of APL's calyx synapses sit on a microglomerulus by this rule; the rest are on KC dendrites away from claws or on PN axons away from boutons.
APLcalyx APL synapseson microglomeruli of a glomerulusPN→APLAPL→PNKC→APLAPL→KCmicroglomeruli

Glomeruli with at least 20 such synapses in every APL are kept: 53 glomeruli.

3Step 3: weighted mean distance between two glomeruli

The distance between glomeruli AAA and BBB is the mean geodesic distance over all pairs of their synapses, each pair weighted by the product of the two synapse weights:

D(A,B)=∑s∈SA∑t∈SBws wt d(s,t)∑s∈SAws∑t∈SBwt(1)D(A, B) = \frac{\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_A}\sum_{t \in \mathcal{S}_B} w_s\, w_t\, d(s, t)}{\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_A} w_s \sum_{t \in \mathcal{S}_B} w_t} \tag{1}D(A,B)=∑s∈SA​​ws​∑t∈SB​​wt​∑s∈SA​​∑t∈SB​​ws​wt​d(s,t)​(1)

Computing every d(s,t)d(s, t)d(s,t) would take 10⁸–10⁹ shortest paths. On a tree there is an exact shortcut. A path between sss and ttt uses edge eee exactly when sss and ttt lie on opposite sides of eee. Summing over edges instead of over pairs gives

D(A,B)=∑eℓe[αe(1−βe)+(1−αe) βe](2)D(A, B) = \sum_{e} \ell_e \left[\alpha_e (1 - \beta_e) + (1 - \alpha_e)\, \beta_e\right] \tag{2}D(A,B)=e∑​ℓe​[αe​(1−βe​)+(1−αe​)βe​](2)
αe\alpha_eαe​, βe\beta_eβe​ = share of AAA's and BBB's synapse weight in the subtree below edge eee; one pass over the tree gives all of them

αe(1−βe)+(1−αe)βe\alpha_e(1-\beta_e) + (1-\alpha_e)\beta_eαe​(1−βe​)+(1−αe​)βe​ is the weighted share of (s,t)(s, t)(s,t) pairs that sit on opposite sides of eee. The result was checked against shortest paths computed directly (Dijkstra) on random synapse sets and agrees to 10⁻¹². Two weightings are reported:

  • All synapses: every APL synapse on the microglomeruli counts once, both directions together. D(A,B)=D(B,A)D(A, B) = D(B, A)D(A,B)=D(B,A).
  • Inputs → outputs: sss runs over APL's inputs at AAA (KC→APL, PN→APL) and ttt over its outputs at BBB (APL→KC, APL→PN). The pair weight is then input synapses × output synapses, Yang's idea of multiplying the two directions, made directional: A→BA \to BA→B is how far AAA's drive to APL has to travel to reach APL's outputs onto BBB.

4Step 4: APL's calyx arbor comes in sub-arbors

Within the calyx, APL's skeleton falls into a few connected pieces that join each other only through the peduncle or the lobes. To find them, skeleton nodes within 5 µm of a calyx APL synapse are called calyx nodes, and the skeleton is restricted to them. Pieces that hold at least 2% of the synapses on microglomeruli are named S1, S2, … by size. Two synapses in the same sub-arbor are much closer along APL than two in different ones.

5Step 5: the glomerulus × glomerulus distances

  • Long paths. Median DDD between different glomeruli: 156 µm (hemibrain R), 230 µm (male CNS L), 155 µm (male CNS R). That is 6.1, 10.1, 6.0 times the straight-line distance between the same synapses.
  • Bands, not blocks. A glomerulus's distance to all others mostly tracks how much of it sits in the main sub-arbor, which makes whole rows and columns light or dark.
  • Not conserved. Over glomerulus pairs, Spearman between APLs: hemibrain R vs male CNS L 0.31; hemibrain R vs male CNS R 0.37; male CNS L vs male CNS R 0.08.
  • Inputs → outputs is close to the all-synapse version; A→BA \to BA→B and B→AB \to AB→A differ by 6–12 µm (median).

6Step 6: self versus cross, and an illustration with passive decay

If APL's signal decayed passively as e−d/λe^{-d/\lambda}e−d/λ with path length, the coupling from APL's inputs at AAA to its outputs at BBB would be

Cλ(A→B)=∑s∈in(A)∑t∈out(B)e−d(s,t)/λ∣in(A)∣  ∣out(B)∣(3)C_\lambda(A \to B) = \frac{\sum_{s \in \mathrm{in}(A)} \sum_{t \in \mathrm{out}(B)} e^{-d(s,t)/\lambda}}{|\mathrm{in}(A)|\;|\mathrm{out}(B)|} \tag{3}Cλ​(A→B)=∣in(A)∣∣out(B)∣∑s∈in(A)​∑t∈out(B)​e−d(s,t)/λ​(3)
computed exactly on the tree in two passes (children to parents, then parents to children); 1 would mean every input sits on every output

This is an illustration only. APL's length constant is not known, and a real cable also loses signal at branch points and depends on neurite diameter, which skeletons do not carry. The ratio of the self term to the mean cross term says how much more a glomerulus's KCs inhibit their own glomerulus than another (Figure 4b).

7Second version: synapses outside the official ROIs added

Following the decision to keep both versions (2026-10-14), the analysis was repeated with synapses outside the official ROIs added (Report 02). Median distances between glomeruli: 162 µm (hemibrain R), 236 µm (male CNS L), 158 µm (male CNS R) (official: 156, 230, 155 µm). All files are in with_outside_ROI_synapses/apl_geodesic/.

Caveats

The sub-arbor split depends on the skeleton's connectivity. A connection missed by the segmentation, or a false merge, would change it, so the sub-arbors are worth checking in neuroglancer before relying on them.

Synapse counts stand in for synaptic strength, and the passive decay ignores branching and diameter.

The skeleton nodes are 0.4 µm (hemibrain) and 0.7 µm (male CNS) apart on median; distances are exact on the skeleton, not on the membrane.
